The Cedar waxwing (Bombycilla cedrorum) is a primarily frugivorous passerine that exhibits a relatively fast-paced life history compared to many other birds of similar body size. Incubation of the eggs at a steady temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] typically lasts for a period of 12 days [ab = 12 days], after which the altricial nestlings emerge. At the moment of hatching, these chicks have a wet weight of just 2.7 grams [Wwb = 2.7 grams], a remarkably small initial mass that necessitates intensive and continuous parental brooding to maintain thermoregulatory stability. This initial weight is a critical starting point for the rapid growth phase that characterizes the nestling period, during which the chicks must accumulate sufficient tissue mass and develop functional flight feathers before they can achieve independence from the nest.

Under the elevated body temperatures characteristic of active metabolic periods at approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the developmental milestones of the Cedar waxwing proceed in a predictable sequence. The fledging event, defined as the time when the young bird first achieves sustained flight and leaves the nest cavity, occurs at 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This is a relatively short nestling period, which is typical for songbirds that are subject to high rates of nest predation. Following departure, the fledglings remain dependent on their parents for food for a further several weeks as they refine their foraging skills for catching insects and identifying fruit-bearing shrubs before they achieve complete nutritional independence from the provisioning adults.

A significant life-history transition is the attainment of reproductive maturity, a process that unfolds under the species' typical active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Puberty, or the onset of gonadal development and the capacity to produce viable gametes, occurs approximately 42 days after hatching [tp = approximately 42 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This rapid maturation, reached in less than two months from fledging, is consistent with the species' need to exploit a temporally variable fruit supply during its first breeding season. The swift completion of sexual maturation allows first-year birds to potentially contribute to the breeding population in the same calendar year of their birth, a strategy that maximizes lifetime reproductive output in an environment where adult mortality can be substantial due to predation and unpredictable winter food availability.

The Cedar waxwing's potential lifespan under natural conditions is relatively modest for a passerine of its size. Field records and recapture data indicate that the maximum recorded longevity is approximately 12.6 years [am = approximately 12.6 years] when the bird's body is functioning at its standard active temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. While few individuals survive to this upper limit, this extended potential lifespan allows for multiple breeding attempts over the course of a bird's life. The species typically produces two to six eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two to six eggs per clutch] in a single nesting attempt, and environmental conditions permitting, they may successfully raise a single brood each year [F_R_i = single brood each year], although a second brood is not uncommon in years with abundant late-summer fruit crops.

The onset of an individual's first reproductive effort is a carefully timed event that aligns with the peak availability of its primary food resources. Under the thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] typical of an active breeding adult, the first successful nesting attempt occurs approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching]. This means that birds hatched in a given summer will initiate their first brood during the following spring or early summer, giving them a full year to complete their own growth and accumulate the necessary energy reserves for egg production and incubation. Female Cedar waxwings reach an adult body mass averaging 31.8 grams [Wwi = 31.8 grams], a size that is sufficient to support the energetic demands of producing a full clutch while also defending a territory.
